title: This world as practice
hook: many teachers say the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure here

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pure Land in the West: temples with pews, lanterns over a parking lot, the name said far from Asia. Your line was far from home. What did you notice that someone had carried a long way? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

Shariputra had a worry, and in the Vimalakirti Sutra he keeps it to himself. If a buddha's land is pure when his mind is pure, he wonders, then why does this world look the way it does? Hills and pits, thorns and gravel, dirt and mess. The Buddha hears the thought anyway. He presses the ground with his toe, and for a moment the whole world shows itself covered in jewels. Then he says, more or less: it was always like this. You just weren't seeing it. Today: this world as practice.
screen: `SHARIPUTRA'S QUIET WORRY.` → `A TOE PRESSES THE GROUND.` → `THIS WORLD AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: First, the line that sets it up. Just before that scene, the Vimalakirti Sutra has the Buddha say, in effect, that a bodhisattva who wants a pure land should purify the mind, because as the mind is purified, the land is purified. Some teachers in East Asia read the Pure Land sutras with that line in their ear. The land of bliss in the west is real to them, and it also points at something closer: a mind made pure, here. Second, the toe. Shariputra wasn't wrong about the gravel. The sutra doesn't say the thorns are imaginary. It says the same ground looks different depending on who is looking. The work isn't to move somewhere cleaner. It's to see this place clearly. Third, an older echo. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, sums up the teaching in one breath: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Purifying the mind isn't a Pure Land invention. The same plain instruction sits in the Dhammapada, in a verse that says nothing about a land in the west. Fourth, what this looks like on a Tuesday. A pure mind, here, isn't a spotless mind. It's a moment met without the extra layer: the grudge, the rush, the story about how this shouldn't be happening. Washing a pan without resenting it. Answering a message without the sharp edge. For these teachers, that small clean moment is a glimpse of the land itself. Tomorrow, we'll hear how Pure Land teachers answer differently about where the land really is.
screen: `AS THE MIND IS PURE, THE LAND IS PURE.` · `THE SAME GROUND, SEEN CLEARLY.` · `AN OLDER ECHO: PURIFY ONE'S MIND.` · `ONE CLEAN MOMENT, HERE.` · then, large: `PURE HERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Pick one moment that's coming up in the next few minutes: the next sip of water, the next step, the next breath. When it comes, do just that one thing, with nothing added. No commentary, no hurry, no complaint. Only the water, only the step, only the breath. Then do it again with the next one. If a grudge or a worry slips in, notice it and let the next breath be clean. The bell holds the time.
This world as practice. The teaching that the Pure Land also points to a mind made pure right here, so ordinary ground becomes the place of practice. Today's word.
Your line: pure here. Today, choose one small chore you usually rush or resent, and do it once with nothing added. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

screen: `DAY 1273 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: MANY VIEWS OF THE LAND.`

howItsDone: Some Pure Land and Chan teachers in East Asia pair calling Amitabha's name with the teaching, from the Vimalakirti Sutra, that as the mind is purified the land is purified, so daily life itself becomes a place of practice.

fork.setup: you're Shariputra. this world looks full of thorns and gravel, and you wonder why. the Buddha presses the ground with his toe. what does he show you?
options: a cleaner world somewhere else, to move to.
this same world, covered in jewels.
that the thorns were never there.
fork.reveal: the world shows itself covered in jewels, and the Buddha says it was always like this. the change is in the seeing, not the place.

original.note: Sanskrit: buddhakshetra, a buddha-field, the land around a buddha. Sukhavati is Amitabha's.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Pure Land is a faraway place you go after you die.
what it means: for some teachers it is that, and it also points at a mind made pure, here, on this same ground.
what a scholar hears: the Vimalakirti Sutra's line, as the mind is purified, the land is purified, read alongside the Pure Land sutras.

sources.ref: Vimalakirti Sutra, chapter 1 (Buddha-land purification; the Buddha touches the ground with his toe)

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East X)
sources.quoted: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.

notes: Vimalakirti Sutra chapter 1 is paraphrased (no public-domain translation used): check the summary of Shariputra's doubt, the toe pressing the ground, and the Buddha's reply.
Dhammapada 183 in Max Müller 1881: confirm exact wording, including the parenthetical '(all)'.

'Some teachers in East Asia read the Pure Land sutras with that line in their ear' rests on the index hook ('many teachers say'); a Keeper may want names (e.g. Chan-Pure Land teachers) or a softer phrase.
Superlatives about the Dhammapada were removed on purpose.
Sanskrit buddhakshetra (बुद्धक्षेत्र): confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
Editor pass: removed the unsourced claim that Pure Land teachers drew on the Dhammapada; now says only that the same instruction appears there.
